---
title: "Analysis 1: linear model per gene (male vs female)"
format: html
execute:
  warning: false
---

## Load libraries

```{r}
#| message: false
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("ggrepel")
```

## Data

We use the TCGA acute myeloid leukemia cohort (TCGA-LAML; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013). The files were downloaded from the GDC hub on UCSC Xena (Goldman et al. 2020).

## Load data

The wide file has around 20,000 gene columns, so one line does not fit in the default read buffer. We make the buffer bigger before reading.

From the probemap we take the gene symbol and the chromosome. We need the chromosome later to split the genes on X and Y from the autosomal ones.

```{r}
#| message: false
Sys.setenv("VROOM_CONNECTION_SIZE" = "5000000")

dat <- read_tsv("../data/processed/03_dat_aug.tsv.gz")

probemap <- read_tsv(
  "../data/raw/gencode_v36_gene_probemap.tsv"
) |>
  select(gene = id,
         symbol = gene,
         chrom)
```

## Model

Every patient has only one sample, so the design is not paired. For each gene we fit `log2_expr ~ gender + age`. We add age as a covariate, so that an age difference between the two groups does not show up as a gender effect.

female is the reference level, which means the gender coefficient is male minus female.

```{r}
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, levels = c("female", "male")))

dat |>
  count(gender)
```

## Long format

```{r}
dat_long <- dat |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("ENSG"),
               names_to = "gene",
               values_to = "log2_expr")
```

For testing we can run on 100 random genes only. With `test_run` set to FALSE all genes are used (this has to be FALSE in the final render).

```{r}
test_run <- FALSE

if (test_run) {
  set.seed(42)
  some_genes <- dat_long |>
    distinct(gene) |>
    slice_sample(n = 100)

  dat_long <- dat_long |>
    semi_join(some_genes, by = "gene")
}
```

## Nest by gene

```{r}
dat_nested <- dat_long |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  nest()

dat_nested
```

## One model per gene

```{r}
dat_nested <- dat_nested |>
  mutate(model_object = map(data,
                            ~ lm(log2_expr ~ gender + age, data = .x)))
```

## Tidy the models

```{r}
dat_nested <- dat_nested |>
  mutate(model_object_tidy = map(model_object,
                                 ~ tidy(.x,
                                        conf.int = TRUE,
                                        conf.level = 0.95)))
```

## Unnest and keep the gender term

```{r}
lm_results <- dat_nested |>
  unnest(model_object_tidy) |>
  filter(term == "gendermale") |>
  select(gene, estimate, std.error, statistic,
         p.value, conf.low, conf.high) |>
  ungroup()
```

## Add gene symbols and chromosome

```{r}
lm_results <- lm_results |>
  left_join(probemap, by = "gene") |>
  mutate(sex_chrom = chrom %in% c("chrX", "chrY")) |>
  relocate(symbol, chrom, sex_chrom, .after = gene)

lm_results |>
  filter(is.na(symbol)) |>
  count(name = "n_without_symbol")
```

## Multiple testing

```{r}
lm_results <- lm_results |>
  mutate(q_value = p.adjust(p.value, method = "fdr"),
         is_significant = case_when(q_value < 0.05 ~ "yes",
                                    TRUE ~ "no"))
```

The values are log2(CPM+1), so they are already normalised for library size. This means the estimate is the log2 fold change of male vs female, e.g. an estimate of 2 is roughly 4 times higher expression in males.

## Direction of change

A gene is Up or Down if q \< 0.05 and \|log2FC\| \> 1, otherwise it is NS. Up is higher in males and Down is higher in females.

```{r}
lm_results <- lm_results |>
  mutate(direction = case_when(q_value < 0.05 & estimate > 1 ~ "Up",
                               q_value < 0.05 & estimate < -1 ~ "Down",
                               TRUE ~ "NS"))

lm_results
```

Here we check if any q values are rounded to 0, since -log10(0) is Inf and those points would be lost in the volcano plot.

```{r}
lm_results |>
  filter(q_value == 0) |>
  count()
```

## Save results

```{r}
write_tsv(lm_results, "../data/processed/05_dat_lm_results.tsv.gz")

lm_summary <- lm_results |>
  count(direction, sex_chrom)

lm_summary

write_tsv(lm_summary, "../data/processed/05_n_up_down.tsv")

n_tested <- nrow(lm_results)
n_changed <- lm_results |>
  filter(direction != "NS") |>
  nrow()
n_changed_sex <- lm_results |>
  filter(direction != "NS",
         sex_chrom) |>
  nrow()
n_signif_auto <- lm_results |>
  filter(q_value < 0.05,
         !sex_chrom) |>
  nrow()
auto_changed <- lm_results |>
  filter(direction != "NS",
         !sex_chrom) |>
  pull(symbol)
n_rps4x_pseudo <- lm_results |>
  filter(q_value < 0.05,
         !sex_chrom,
         str_detect(symbol, "^RPS4XP")) |>
  nrow()
```

We tested `r format(n_tested, big.mark = ",")` genes in total. Using q \< 0.05 and \|log2FC\| \> 1, `r n_changed` genes are different between males and females, and `r n_changed_sex` of these are on X or Y. If we drop the fold change cut-off, `r n_signif_auto` autosomal genes have q \< 0.05.

## Volcano plot

We label the 10 significant genes with the lowest q value and also the significant autosomal genes. Genes without a symbol get their Ensembl ID.

```{r}
top_genes <- lm_results |>
  filter(direction != "NS") |>
  arrange(q_value) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

volcano_dat <- lm_results |>
  mutate(gene_group = case_when(direction == "NS" ~ "Not significant",
                                sex_chrom ~ "Significant, X/Y",
                                TRUE ~ "Significant, autosomal"),
         label = case_when(gene %in% pull(top_genes, gene) |
                             gene_group == "Significant, autosomal" ~
                             coalesce(symbol, gene),
                           TRUE ~ ""))

volcano_plot <- volcano_dat |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate,
             y = -log10(pmax(q_value, 1e-300)),
             colour = gene_group,
             label = label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = volcano_dat |>
               filter(gene_group == "Significant, autosomal"),
             size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(data = volcano_dat |>
                    filter(label != ""),
                  size = 3,
                  max.overlaps = Inf,
                  show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Not significant" = "grey70",
                                 "Significant, X/Y" = "firebrick",
                                 "Significant, autosomal" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change (male vs female)",
       y = "-log10(q value)",
       colour = "",
       title = "Differential expression, male vs female (AML)") +
  theme_minimal()

volcano_plot

ggsave("../results/05_volcano.png", volcano_plot, width = 7, height = 5)
```

One point is one gene. On the x axis is the log2 fold change (male vs female), on the y axis -log10 of the q value, so higher up means more significant. The dashed lines are the cut-offs we used (q \< 0.05 and \|log2FC\| \> 1). The grey points do not pass both cut-offs. Some of them do have q \< 0.05, but their fold change is smaller than 2.

Nearly all the genes with a big difference are on the sex chromosomes. XIST, which comes from the inactive X, is much higher in females. Y genes like DDX3Y, KDM5D, UTY and RPS4Y1 are higher in males. We expected this, because XIST and Y genes like RPS4Y1 are used as sex markers in RNA data (van den Berge and Sijen 2017). So it is also a good check that the analysis and the sex labels of the samples are right. Only one autosomal gene passes both cut-offs (`r auto_changed`), and it is labelled in the plot.

## Forest plot of top autosomal genes

We expect the biggest differences to be on X and Y. To see if anything happens in the rest of the genome, we plot the 10 autosomal genes with the lowest q value.

```{r}
top_auto <- lm_results |>
  filter(!sex_chrom) |>
  arrange(q_value) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

forest_plot <- top_auto |>
  mutate(symbol = coalesce(symbol, gene),
         symbol = fct_reorder(symbol, estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = symbol, colour = is_significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                orientation = "y",
                width = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("no" = "grey50",
                                 "yes" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change, male vs female (95% CI)",
       y = "",
       colour = "q < 0.05",
       title = "Top 10 autosomal genes") +
  theme_minimal()

forest_plot

ggsave("../results/05_forest.png", forest_plot, width = 6, height = 4)
```

`r n_signif_auto` autosomal genes have q \< 0.05, but for most of them the fold change is small. `r n_rps4x_pseudo` of these are RPS4X pseudogenes. Their sequence is very close to RPS4X on X and RPS4Y1 on Y, so we think the signal most likely comes from reads of the sex chromosome genes that map to the pseudogenes, and not from a real difference on the autosomes. Reads that map to more than one place, for example to a gene and its processed pseudogene, are known to make genes look expressed when they are not (Zhang et al. 2013).

So in our cohort the expression differences between males and females are found almost only on the sex chromosomes.

## Limitations

Other studies did find sex differences in AML, for example in which mutations occur together and in gene expression inside mutation groups (Hellesøy et al. 2021; Ozga et al. 2024). They had bigger cohorts and looked within genetic subgroups, like patients with FLT3-ITD. We compare all 151 patients in one model and we have no mutation data, so if a difference only exists inside a subgroup we would not see it.
